procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Madras directing a sum of Rs. 500, deposited as security for the appellant's appearance in contempt of court proceedings, to be adjusted against the fine imposed upon him in those proceedings.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Contempt of court proceedings (No. 3 of 1962) were initiated against the appellant in the High Court of Madras due to a letter he wrote to the Chief Justice containing remarks about the dismissal of his revision application. The High Court found him guilty of contempt and sentenced him to six months' imprisonment and a fine. He served the imprisonment but did not pay the fine. The High Court dismissed the appellant's application for refund of the deposited amount and allowed the State's application for payment of the amount towards satisfaction of the unpaid fine.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, by special leave, appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order. The appellant argued that the State's application to adjust the deposit towards the fine was time-barred under Section 70 of the Penal Code. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 70 of the Penal Code did not apply because the law of contempt of court, as administered by the High Court, is a special law.

directions: There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself is a special jurisdiction derived from the Constitution, and therefore not governed by the Penal Code or the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: An appellant was found guilty of contempt of the High Court and sentenced to imprisonment and a fine.
The appellant served the imprisonment but did not pay the fine.
More than six years later, the State sought to recover the unpaid fine from a security deposit the appellant had made in court.
The appellant argued that under Section 70 of the Penal Code, the collection of the fine was barred by a six-year limitation period.

law.description: Declares that every High Court is a 'court of record' and shall have all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
An Act that regulates the jurisdiction and procedure for contempt of court. The Court found that this Act assumes the pre-existence of the High Court's power, rather than creating it.
Provides that a fine can only be levied within six years after the passing of the sentence.
States that the provisions of the Penal Code relating to fines (including Section 70) apply to all fines imposed under any 'Act, Regulation, rule or bye-law'.

application.description: The Court first identified the source of the High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself. It held that this power does not come from any legislative act, such as the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952.

Instead, the Court found that the power is vested directly in the High Court by Article 215 of the Constitution, which makes every High Court a 'court of record' with the inherent power to punish for its own contempt.

Because the power is constitutional, the Court described it as a 'special jurisdiction' that cannot be taken away or conferred afresh by a legislature. The Contempt of Courts Act, therefore, only assumes the existence of this power and places certain restrictions on it (like setting maximum penalties), but it does not create the jurisdiction.

The Court then addressed the appellant's argument that Section 70 of the Penal Code should apply via Section 25 of the General Clauses Act. It reasoned that Section 25 only applies to fines imposed 'under any Act'. Since the High Court's power to punish for its own contempt derives from the Constitution and not the Contempt of Courts Act, the fine was not imposed 'under any Act'.

As a result, the condition for applying Section 25 of the General Clauses Act was not met. This meant that the limitations in the Penal Code, including the six-year time bar in Section 70, were not applicable to the collection of the fine.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself is a special jurisdiction derived directly from Article 215 of the Constitution, not from the Contempt of Courts Act. Therefore, this jurisdiction is not governed by the Penal Code or the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the six-year limitation for collecting a fine under the Penal Code does not apply.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its special jurisdiction for contempt, has the incidental power to order the satisfaction of a fine from a security deposit made by the contemnor in the same proceedings.

facts: A person (the appellant) was found guilty of contempt of court and sentenced to imprisonment and a fine.
The appellant had previously made a security deposit of Rs. 500 to ensure his presence during the contempt proceedings.
The High Court ordered that the unpaid fine be satisfied by using the money from this security deposit.
law: The High Court is a "court of record" and is vested with a "special jurisdiction" to handle contempt of court cases.
This special jurisdiction includes all "incidental and necessary powers" required to make that jurisdiction effective.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the security deposit was initially made for the specific purpose of securing the appellant's presence.

However, the Court reasoned that because the High Court has incidental and necessary powers to enforce its special contempt jurisdiction, it could use any available fund belonging to the contemnor to satisfy a fine it had imposed.
The power to order the satisfaction of the fine from the security deposit was considered one of these necessary incidental powers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court, as part of its special jurisdiction for contempt, had the incidental power to order that the fine it imposed be satisfied from the security deposit made by the contemnor in the same case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself is a special jurisdiction derived from the Constitution, and therefore not governed by the Penal Code or the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The order imposing the fine was passed under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952.
Under Section 25 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the provisions of Sections 63 to 70 of the Penal Code apply to all fines imposed under any 'Act'.
Therefore, Section 70 of the Penal Code, which sets a six-year limitation period for levying a fine, applies to this case.
Since more than six years had passed, the State's application to collect the fine from the deposit was time-barred.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's power to punish for contempt is a special jurisdiction derived from Article 215 of the Constitution, which makes every High Court a 'court of record' with the power to punish for contempt of itself.
This power is not derived from the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952; the Act merely assumes and regulates this pre-existing constitutional power.
The law of contempt is a 'special law' as defined in Section 41 of the Penal Code.
According to Section 5 of the Penal Code, its provisions (including the time limit in Section 70) do not affect the provisions of any special law.
Therefore, the six-year limitation period in Section 70 of the Penal Code does not apply, and there is no time bar for the recovery of the fine.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its special jurisdiction for contempt, has the incidental power to order the satisfaction of a fine from a security deposit made by the contemnor in the same proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The security deposit was made for a specific and particular purpose, which was to secure the appellant's presence during the contempt proceedings.
respondent_arguments: As a court of record with a special jurisdiction for contempt, the High Court possesses all incidental and necessary powers to effectuate that jurisdiction.
This includes the power to order the satisfaction of a fine it has imposed from any available fund deposited by, or for the benefit of, the appellant in the same proceedings.

cases.case_name: Sukhdev Singh Sodhi v. The Chief Justice and Judges of the Pepsu High Court
cases.principle: Section 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952, does not confer a new jurisdiction but assumes the pre-existence of a High Court's right to punish for contempt and its special practice and procedure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself is a special jurisdiction derived from its status as a Court of Record under Article 215 of the Constitution, not from the Contempt of Courts Act or the Penal Code. This power constitutes a special law, and therefore, the provisions of the Penal Code, including any limitation period for the collection of fines, do not apply to fines imposed for contempt of a High Court.
obiter: A High Court, as a court of record being clothed with a special jurisdiction, has all incidental and necessary powers to effectuate that jurisdiction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's power to punish for contempt of itself is a special jurisdiction that originates directly from Article 215 of the Constitution, which designates it as a 'court of record'. This power is not derived from or conferred by the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952, which merely assumes and regulates this pre-existing constitutional authority. Consequently, this special jurisdiction is not governed by the provisions of the Penal Code or the Code of Criminal Procedure, including any limitation periods for the recovery of fines.
legal_tests_applied: The court determined the source of the High Court's contempt power by analyzing whether it was statutory (derived from the Contempt of Courts Act) or constitutional (derived from Article 215).

The court applied the doctrine of incidental powers, which holds that a court vested with a special jurisdiction also possesses all necessary and incidental powers to effectively execute that jurisdiction.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's premise that the power to punish for contempt arose from the Contempt of Courts Act was incorrect; the court held the power is constitutional, stemming from Article 215.

Because the power is not derived from a statute like the Contempt of Courts Act, Section 25 of the General Clauses Act (which would apply the Penal Code's provisions to fines imposed under an 'Act') is inapplicable.

As a result, the six-year limitation period for recovering a fine under Section 70 of the Penal Code does not apply to a fine imposed under the High Court's special constitutional jurisdiction for contempt.

The argument that the security deposit was for a specific purpose was overcome by the court's finding that its incidental powers, necessary to effectuate its special jurisdiction, allowed it to order satisfaction of the fine from any available fund deposited by the appellant in the same proceedings.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the High Court's jurisdiction to punish for its own contempt is a special one, not arising from the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952, but from its constitutional status as a 'court of record' under Article 215.
The court agreed that the Contempt of Courts Act does not confer a new jurisdiction but 'assumes... the. existence of a right to punish for contempt in every High Court'.
Because the jurisdiction is a special one and not within the purview of the Penal Code, the limitation period in Section 70 of the Penal Code is not an impediment to the recovery of the fine.

The court affirmed that as a court of record with a special jurisdiction, the High Court possesses 'all incidental and necessary powers to effectuate that jurisdiction,' which includes the power to order the satisfaction of a fine from a security deposit made in the same case.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the constitutional principle that the power of a High Court, as a court of record, to punish for its own contempt is inherent and vested by the Constitution itself, and therefore no Act of a legislature can take away that jurisdiction or confer it afresh.
